nameStory: Wood anemone gets its name from its love of woodland habitats, while its alternate name 'windflower' comes from the Greek word 'anemos' meaning wind. Early botanists noticed how these delicate flowers seem to dance and sway with every gentle breeze that filters through the forest canopy.
description: Wood anemone is a charming spring wildflower that carpets the forest floor with small white blooms before the trees leaf out. This low-growing perennial reaches only 4-8 inches tall and spreads by underground stems to form colonies. Each plant produces a single delicate white flower above a whorl of three deeply divided leaves, creating an elegant woodland display that signals winter's end.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Single white flower per plant with 5 white petal-like sepals (no true petals) and a cluster of yellow stamens in the center. The flower feels papery-thin and closes on cloudy days.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three leaves arranged in a circle around the stem, each divided into 3 sharply-toothed leaflets. The leaves feel thin and delicate with prominent veins you can trace with your finger.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing plant 4-8 inches tall that often forms patches or colonies. Each plant has just one flower stem rising from the center of the leaf whorl.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Slender, smooth green stems that feel soft and slightly hollow when gently squeezed. The flower stem rises directly from where the three leaves meet.

habitat: Wood anemone thrives in rich, moist deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, particularly under maples, oaks, and birches. Look for it on gentle slopes and in woodland valleys where leaf litter creates deep, fertile soil. It's especially common in areas that receive dappled sunlight in early spring before the canopy fills in.

seasonality.spring: Flowers bloom from April to early May, often appearing before leaves fully emerge on trees above. The white blooms are most visible and identification is easiest during this peak flowering period.
seasonality.summer: Leaves remain green through summer but become less noticeable as other vegetation fills in. Plants focus on storing energy in their underground rhizomes during this time.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may turn yellowish before dying back completely. By late fall, only the underground portions remain alive and ready for next spring.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant with no above-ground parts visible. Only the underground rhizome system survives, spreading slowly to form next year's colony.

funFact: Despite being called 'five-leaved' in its scientific name (quinquefolia), wood anemone actually has only three leaves - each divided into three leaflets, making botanists who named it centuries ago look a bit foolish for their hasty counting!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with bloodroot, which also has white spring flowers in woodlands. Remember: wood anemone has three leaves in a whorl around the stem, while bloodroot has one large, deeply-lobed leaf that wraps around the flower stem at the base.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this North American wood anemone with the European wood anemone (Anemonoides nemorosa) that shares the same common names. Our native species is specifically adapted to New England's forests and has slightly different leaf shapes and growth patterns than its European cousin.
compareHints: Wood anemone is the most common Anemonoides species in New England, while its relatives like Greek anemone and yellow anemone are primarily garden escapees rarely found in the wild. Unlike those colorful cousins, our native wood anemone is always white and blooms earlier in the season. The white flowers and three-part leaf arrangement make it instantly recognizable among its genus.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Greek Anemone stands out from its New England relatives by having the most petals (10-15) and the most color variety, including true blue flowers which the native Wood Anemones lack.
Wood anemone differs from its American relative, the five-leaved wood anemone, primarily in flower structure - it typically has 6-8 white sepals instead of exactly 5.
Yellow anemone is the only yellow-flowered member of its genus in New England, making it fairly easy to distinguish from its relatives.
Among its anemone relatives in New England, blue anemone stands out for its blue flowers (wood anemones are white or pinkish) and notably hairy leaf undersides.
